question: Who is addressed by the command to say this?

positions.position: Muhammad addresses the people of Mecca, the unbelieving idolaters.
positions.reasons: Muqatil names the Meccans; Bursevi and Alusi describe the address as rebuke and confutation.

question: What does أَرَءَيْتُم mean here?

positions.position: Tell me or inform me.
positions.reasons: Nasafi, Bursevi, Alusi, and Tabatabai use this gloss; Biqai says the question probes the idols' status, already visibly apparent.

question: How is أَرَءَيْتُم read?

positions.position: A reading adds kaf: araʾaytkum or araytkum.
positions.reasons: Farra reports Abdullah's practice also at 107:1; Jishumi identifies Ibn Masud's codex; Alusi records the variant.

positions.position: The common reading is araʾaytum.
positions.reasons: Jishumi cites regional codices; Nahhas calls araytum a familiar Arabic reduction of original araʾaytum and notes another dialect softens the second hamza.

positions.position: A reading deletes the hamza.
positions.reasons: Zajjaj records omitted alif; Qiraat-ER calls deletion a mutawatir Hijazi simplification from raʾa to raytum.

positions.position: A mutawatir reading softens the hamza to an intermediate sound.
positions.reasons: Qiraat-ER distinguishes this from deletion.

positions.position: A mutawatir reading lengthens the vowel before the hamza.
positions.reasons: Qiraat-ER notes its deliberative prosody.

turns_on: How the hamza is retained, softened, deleted, or supplemented with kaf.

question: How do أَرَءَيْتُم, أَرُونِى, and the questions fit together syntactically?

positions.position: أَرَءَيْتُم is transitive: ما تدعون is its first object and the creation question its second; أَرُونِى reinforces 'tell me'.
positions.reasons: Bursevi says both objects ask the alleged gods' status; Samin and Alusi give the emphatic analysis; Abu Hayyan notes an alternative with omitted second object.

positions.position: أَرَءَيْتُم is an intransitive attention-getter and ما تدعون begins a rebuking question.
positions.reasons: Ibn Atiyya allows this; Samin attributes it to Akhfash and compares 18:63; Alusi repeats it.

positions.position: The two verbs compete for the creation question, with the later governing and an object omitted from the first.
positions.reasons: Abu Hayyan prefers this; Samin reports the shared-object construction; Alusi records Abu Hayyan's preference.

positions.position: أَرُونِى begins a fresh challenge about the idols' status.
positions.reasons: Biqai argues the idols can already be seen, so 'show me' asks their status rather than mere sight.

positions.position: أَرُونِى is an appositive of inclusion to أَرَءَيْتُم.
positions.reasons: Alusi records this unnamed analysis.

turns_on: Whether the first verb takes objects, is an attention-getter, or shares government with the second.

question: What beings are called upon besides God?

positions.position: Idols or false gods worshipped by the polytheists.
positions.reasons: Zajjaj calls them claimed deities; Muqatil names al-Lat, al-Uzza, Manat; Razi, Qurtubi, Nasafi, and Tabatabai say idols; Alusi prefers the broader class of all false deities; Study Quran includes jinn.

positions.position: Angels worshipped by the Meccans.
positions.reasons: Muqatil identifies them as the deities addressed.

positions.position: Idols, celestial bodies, and other worshipped objects.
positions.reasons: Bursevi explicitly broadens the referents.

positions.position: All beings to which people assign independent existence or causal force.
positions.reasons: Qashani gives this inwardly inflected referent and asks what they independently or jointly affect.

turns_on: Whether the referents are idols, angels, celestial bodies, jinn, or all claimed deities.

question: Why does the verse use plural personal verbs or the reading من for these objects?

positions.position: Personal plural agreement reflects the worshippers' treatment of the idols as rational, honored agents.
positions.reasons: Farra says they were imagined speaking and honored as rulers; Nahhas contrasts ordinary ما with Ibn Masud's personal من; Tabatabai says worshippers attribute rational acts. Nahhas records unanimous masculine plural خلقوا and لهم.

positions.position: Ibn Masud reads من تدعون or من تعبدون in place of ما تدعون.
positions.reasons: Farra gives من تعبدون; Nahhas and Ibn Atiyya report من تدعون; the personal form follows their imagined status.

turns_on: Whether their imagined personhood or ordinary nonrational agreement governs.

question: What does تَدْعُونَ mean here?

positions.position: Worship or invoke as an object of worship.
positions.reasons: Ibn Atiyya glosses it as worship; Alusi agrees. Qashani extends calling to naming and assigning causal power.

question: What does مِن دُونِ ٱللَّهِ convey?

positions.position: Apart from God, beneath the supreme King who has no equal.
positions.reasons: Biqai stresses the disparity of rank.

question: How is مَاذَا خَلَقُوا۟ parsed?

positions.position: ما is interrogative and ذا is extra; the whole phrase is the object of خلقوا.
positions.reasons: Tabatabai gives this analysis; Alusi includes it among three parsings.

positions.position: ماذا is one interrogative object.
positions.reasons: Alusi says on this parse خلقوا supplies the second object of أرأيتم.

positions.position: ما is interrogative and ذا relative, with خلقوا as its clause.
positions.reasons: Alusi says the whole ماذا خلقوا clause then functions as the second object of أرأيتم.

turns_on: Whether ذا is extra, or ما and ذا form one interrogative or a relative construction.

question: What is the challenge about earthly creation?

positions.position: Show any earthly thing or part independently created by the alleged gods; they created nothing and so do not merit worship.
positions.reasons: Muqatil compares God's creation; Tabari says God created the entire earth from nothing; Razi says reason excludes even the smallest thing; Tabarsi and Ibn Kathir link creation to gratitude; Islahi notes idolaters already accepted God as Creator; Kuranyolu says influence presupposes creation.

question: What does مِنَ ٱلْأَرْضِ specify?

positions.position: It is partitive: any portion of earth or what is on its surface.
positions.reasons: Ibn Atiyya says even animals come from earth; Abu Hayyan allows earth's parts or an omitted noun for surface things; Alusi lists parts and regions.

positions.position: It clarifies the otherwise ambiguous ماذا خلقوا.
positions.reasons: Samin and Alusi identify the specifying grammatical function; Tabatabai attaches it to the interrogative.

positions.position: It refers to what is in or on the earth; من can mean في.
positions.reasons: Damghani cites 2:223 and 35:40; Burhan allows this or a genus use, and compares the Friday call.

positions.position: It refers broadly to the lower worlds.
positions.reasons: Alusi prefers this over parts of earth or its surface creatures.

turns_on: Whether it marks a part, things on earth, lower realms, or location.

question: What share in the heavens is denied?

positions.position: A share in creating the heavens with God, which they have none.
positions.reasons: Zajjaj says such creation would justify worship; Qurtubi, Alusi, Tabatabai and others read the question this way. Tabatabai argues governance entails creation, citing 39:38 and 43:87.

positions.position: Any share in heavenly dominion, ownership, control, governance, benefit, harm, or creation.
positions.reasons: Muqatil links 34:22; Qushayri asks about power to help or harm; Biqai includes naturalists' governance; Bursevi includes possession; Ibn Kathir assigns all ownership and control to God.

positions.position: They share nothing in the heavens or earth.
positions.reasons: Tabari says the supposed share would warrant service, but creation belongs only to God.

turns_on: Whether partnership means creation alone, dominion/governance, or any participation.

question: How is أَمْ joined to the first challenge?

positions.position: It is connected to an omitted matching clause: a share in earth or a share in heaven.
positions.reasons: Bursevi prefers this analysis; Alusi records it; Biqai describes the paired omissions as iḥtibāk, with creation supplied for heaven and partnership for earth.

positions.position: It is a disconnected أم introducing a fresh question.
positions.reasons: Samin states this; Alusi allows it.

turns_on: Whether أم is disconnected or connected with an omitted counterpart.

question: Why contrast creation on earth with partnership in the heavens?

positions.position: The pair excludes independent lower-world creation and shared upper-world creation, covering all grounds of worship.
positions.reasons: Biqai identifies reciprocal ellipsis; Alusi says either denial removes their claim; Bursevi names heaven's elevated unsupported structure as conspicuous evidence.

positions.position: The heavens guard against a theory of celestial intermediaries governing earthly events.
positions.reasons: Baydawi notes this possible inference; Bursevi repeats it; Kuranyolu says the unseen heaven receives a thought-provoking question rather than a demand to show it.

positions.position: Heavenly creation is obvious common ground; agency in lower events is disputed.
positions.reasons: Alusi says everyone concedes the first, while apparent human agency makes the second contested.

turns_on: What the upper and lower language brings out.

question: What kind of book is demanded, and what must it show?

positions.position: An earlier revealed scripture that validates worship of idols or their partnership with God.
positions.reasons: Muqatil includes the claim God has a partner; Tabari says proof of creation or a heavenly share; Razi says an alleged divine command requires revelation. Tabatabai names the Torah; Biqai adds Gospel and Psalms, which actually attest oneness; Ibn Ashur says 'come' metaphorically means produce evidence.

positions.position: A scripture predating the Quran affirming God's oneness.
positions.reasons: Baydawi words the requested scripture this way.

turns_on: Whether it must validate idol worship, partnership in creation, or affirm divine oneness.

question: What does مِن قَبْلِ هَٰذَآ modify or identify?

positions.position: It qualifies كتاب: a revealed book before this Quran.
positions.reasons: Abu al-Baqa gives the adjective parse; Qurtubi and Ibn Ashur identify 'this' as Quran.

positions.position: It qualifies an implied more general item: something existing before this.
positions.reasons: Samin prefers the broader ellipsis.

turns_on: Whether it describes the book itself or an implied general proof.

question: Why require the book to predate the Quran?

positions.position: It prevents the opponents from composing a text for the challenge and confronts them with earlier revelation's monotheism.
positions.reasons: Ibn Ashur relates their boast at 8:31; Nasafi, Abu Hayyan, Bursevi, and Razi say all earlier scriptures reject idolatry, Razi calling that widely transmitted knowledge.

question: How is أَثَٰرَةٍ read and formed?

positions.position: Without alif and with moving thāʾ: atharah or atharah, a singular trace or special knowledge.
positions.reasons: Sulami, Ibn Abbas, Ikrima, Qatada, Ali and others are reported; Ibn Jinni and Samin call it singular of athar. Qurtubi and Wahidi associate a vocalization with knowledge specially favored; JZ records Ibn Masud, Abu Razin, Ayyub, Yaqub. Reports vary on specific readers.

positions.position: The common or majority reading has an alif: athārah, a verbal noun on faʿālah.
positions.reasons: Farra compares samāhah; Tabari compares samājah and qabāhah; Ibn Atiyya, Samin and Alusi give verbal-noun formation. Tabari says this is the established Arabic remainder sense.

positions.position: Without alif and with silent thāʾ: athrah, a single transmitted report or trace.
positions.reasons: Farra analogizes rajfah and khaṭfah; Ibn Jinni says demanding even one account strengthens the challenge; reported for Ali, Sulami, Qatada and others. Traditions differ on whether the hamza has fatḥa, ḍamma, or kasra.

positions.position: Other hamza vowels include uthurah and itharah, sometimes with silent thāʾ.
positions.reasons: Kisa'i reports the damma form and is attributed kasra too; Nahhas and Ibn Atiyya preserve variants; Baydawi and Alusi associate itharah with stirring meanings.

positions.position: Another reported reading is 'an inheritance of knowledge' (mīrāth min ʿilm).
positions.reasons: Ikrima is cited by Ibn Atiyya through Thalabi.

turns_on: The presence of alif, hamza vowel, thāʾ vowel, and singular or verbal-noun patterns.

question: What does أَثَٰرَةٍ مِّنْ عِلْمٍ mean?

positions.position: A surviving remnant or trace of earlier knowledge.
positions.reasons: Abu Ubayda, Farra, Ibn Qutayba, Kalbi, Abu Bakr b. Ayyash and many others give this sense. Camel fat and inherited nobility illustrate it in al-Raʿi's poem; Tabari prefers established Arabic usage; Tabatabai notes it remains close to inherited learning.

positions.position: A transmitted report, chain, or inherited teaching from earlier people or prophets.
positions.reasons: Farra allows recovery from earlier books; Mujahid asks for a transmitter, Qurazi an isnad, Muqatil a prophetic report of partnership. Aʿsha's line, Umar's āthiran saying and maʾthūr usage support the sense; Tabatabai prefers Raghib's derivation from following a trace.

positions.position: Written marks, handwriting, or divinatory lines in earth.
positions.reasons: Ibn Abbas and some Prophetic attributions give writing or ground lines; Abu Bakr b. Ayyash calls it divination; Abu Said calls it good handwriting; Sufyan doubts whether Ibn Abbas heard his report from the Prophet. Itqan also reports astrology/divination.

positions.position: Knowledge specially reserved, granted, or privileged for a person or group.
positions.reasons: Qatada, Abu Salama and others derive this from athrah; Wahidi calls this a good reading, and Ibn Atiyya applies it across variants.

positions.position: Knowledge extracted and brought to light.
positions.reasons: Al-Hasan uses the image of drawing something out; Wahidi groups it with root senses; Abu Hayyan says the result is transmitted.

positions.position: A sign, mark, or clear proof concerning their claim.
positions.reasons: Zajjaj gives mark; Ibn Abbas gives clear proof; Ibn Kathir treats diverse glosses as converging on clear proof and says Tabari chose it, though Tabari's own note prefers 'remainder'.

positions.position: An argument, effort, or debate grounded in knowledge.
positions.reasons: Mawardi offers effort and argument; Baydawi and Alusi explain kasra ithārah as stirring meanings in debate.

positions.position: Something attractive to the eye, like a full camel.
positions.reasons: Wahidi reports Mubarrad's additional usage.

turns_on: Whether it is a remnant, transmitted account, special knowledge, a sign, extracted knowledge, writing, divination, or reasoned argument.

question: What does مِّنْ عِلْمٍ add?

positions.position: It qualifies أثارة as actual knowledge, even a small amount, and excludes conjecture.
positions.reasons: Samin makes it an adjective; Alusi says tanwin reduces quantity; Biqai accepts a fragment from necessity, experiment, observation, another source or even conjecture, while Islahi excludes fancy and conjecture.

question: What kinds of proof does the verse demand, and what follows if none is produced?

positions.position: It challenges idolatry with rational evidence from creation and transmitted evidence from scripture or prior learning; absent both, the claim fails.
positions.reasons: Tabarsi distinguishes reason, scripture, report; Qurtubi distinguishes rational and transmitted proof; Razi argues divine command needs revelation and says earlier scripture and prophetic teaching reject idols; Ibn Ashur says the breadth of allowed evidence makes the rebuttal stronger, citing 28:50. Study Quran relates other challenge verses.

positions.position: A rational proof based on sound knowledge could also serve as the requested أثارة.
positions.reasons: Qashani opens the offered evidence to reason; Biqai admits even a fragment; Mawardi mentions argument.

positions.position: God's testimony through revelation or faithfully transmitted prophetic teaching is needed to establish divine partners.
positions.reasons: Islahi says conjecture cannot justify the claim; Razi rejects any supposed command to worship idols in Muhammad's revelation and denies one in prior prophets.

turns_on: How rational, written, oral, and divine testimony support or refute the claim.

question: What is the point of إِن كُنتُمْ صَٰدِقِينَ?

positions.position: It puts the claimants' truthfulness to a test: failure to produce evidence exposes a baseless or false claim.
positions.reasons: Tabari says unsupported claims benefit no one, comparing 2:23; Biqai notes their aversion to lying; Tabatabai demands proof of a share in creation.

question: What does the report of a prophet drawing lines say?

positions.position: A prophet knew line drawing; one who matched his line would know that prophet's knowledge.
positions.reasons: Abd al-Razzaq, Wahidi, Ibn Atiyya, Durr and Alusi transmit the report. Qurtubi says the line report is established through Muawiya b. al-Hakam in Muslim and another sound route, while Ibn al-Arabi and Qurtubi elsewhere call particular Ibn Abbas or matching-line routes unsound.

question: Does the line-drawing report permit geomancy?

positions.position: A genuinely matching line would be valid, or the prophetic precedent permits the practice.
positions.reasons: Ibn Atiyya says many scholars take the apparent conditional this way; Ibn al-Arabi reports a permissive view. Makki describes the prophet's two-finger method; Ibn Abbas details paired erasure and outcomes in Arab al-asham.

positions.position: The practice is prohibited: the prophetic technique has ceased or cannot be verified, and ordinary geomancy claims unseen knowledge.
positions.reasons: Ibn Atiyya reports this view; Khattabi calls the line a past prophetic sign; Qadi Iyad says coincidence cannot be known and law forbids divination; Qurtubi prefers prohibition, describing planetary figures and intent-dependent sin or unbelief.

positions.position: The verse's mention of sand writing is a taunt, not a validation of its proof.
positions.reasons: Abu Hayyan says the gloss either has no evidential force or mocks the idolaters; Alusi relays this conditional reading.

turns_on: Whether matching the prophetic line is possible and whether claims to unseen knowledge are lawful.

question: How does the discussion distinguish omens, dreams, and knowledge of the unseen?

positions.position: Good words and dreams may encourage; bad omens and divinatory augury are forbidden, and God alone knows the unseen.
positions.reasons: Ibn al-Arabi allows dreams as part of prophethood and describes faʾl as proceeding cheerfully after good words while ignoring bad ones. Qurtubi rejects a poet's condemnation of faʾl; the Prophet's prayer denies independent omens. Qurtubi says customary signs can fail, as with date palms.

turns_on: Which signs can guide action and whether they give certainty.

question: Can handwriting itself serve as legal evidence?

positions.position: Recognized handwriting once supported judgments, and authenticated letters, wills, and admissions can be accepted.
positions.reasons: Ibn Khuwayz Mindad reports Malik's early practice and his school's rules when witnesses recognize a judge's letter, will, or debt admission.

positions.position: Malik later abandoned judgment by handwriting when fraud and forgery spread.
positions.reasons: Malik says changed conduct brings changed rulings.

turns_on: The reliability of authenticated writing after forgery spread.

question: How does the root أثر enter the separate discussion of oaths?

positions.position: آثرا means transmitting another person's oath, rather than personally uttering it; swearing by other than God usurps God's supreme reverence.
positions.reasons: Nahhas cites the sound report forbidding oaths by fathers, Umar's resolve, and the distinction from ذاكرا; he interprets kufr as concealing God's due reverence. He also records root uses for raised dust, soft underfoot, and mīthara with waw changed to ya.

question: How does this challenge connect with other verses and the sūrah's argument?

positions.position: It parallels other Qur'anic demands for proof and supports al-Ahqaf's warning to idolaters who trust alleged protectors.
positions.reasons: Wahidi and Ibn Jawzi point to Fatir 35:40; Study Quran cites 2:23, 10:38, 21:24, 37:156-157, 54:43, 68:37 and book challenges in 34:44, 43:21. Islahi says Judgment is certain and intercessors cannot save them.

positions.position: The sūrah continues al-Jathiyah's rebuke and moves from signs of creation to denounced idol worship and rejected revelation.
positions.reasons: Ibn al-Zubayr cites 46:3 and 46:7; Biqai starts by dismantling the alleged protective partners.

positions.position: The sūrah repeatedly warns deniers of Resurrection while arguing divine unity and prophethood.
positions.reasons: Tabatabai cites 46:3, 6, 17, 20, 34, 35, and mentions Ad, neighboring towns, and believing jinn.

question: Where was al-Ahqaf revealed, and how many verses are counted?

positions.position: It is Meccan; one count gives thirty-five verses, while two verses are disputed.
positions.reasons: Durr reports Ibn Abbas and Ibn al-Zubayr for Mecca and gives the thirty-five count; Tabatabai notes two disputed exceptions.

question: What merit is reported for reciting al-Ahqaf?

positions.position: A report promises ten good deeds per grain of sand, ten sins erased, and ten ranks raised.
positions.reasons: Jishumi transmits Ubayy b. Ka'b from the Prophet without stating a grading.

question: What inward meanings are drawn from the verse?

positions.position: Ego and Satan cannot act in the self or spirit; God alone creates and turns hearts.
positions.reasons: Bursevi maps earth to self and heavens to spirit.

positions.position: Sincere worship seeks neither paradise as reward nor escape from Hell.
positions.reasons: Bursevi says even reward- or fear-driven worship regards something besides God; he attributes agreement to outer and inner scholars.

question: What unrelated reading or interpretive notices appear alongside the verse?

positions.position: Readers quiesce nine possessive yāʾs, including the one in Yusuf's يدعونني إليه.
positions.reasons: Nashr records suggested difficulty from many successive letters and notes other explanations.

question: How does al-Khuli's hermeneutic approach understand Quran interpretation?

positions.position: Interpretation is active dialogue shaped by the reader's worldview, culture, expectations, and assumptions; tafsir should use literary and human sciences.
positions.reasons: Rifai-Khuli says al-Khuli criticized sectarian instrumental tafsir, explored sociology and psychology, directed students toward the method, and formed al-Umana with Khalafallah, Bint al-Shati, and al-Alai. Later Arabic writers mainly used it in literary criticism; some experts feared clerical hostility to applying it to scripture.

positions.position: Religious thought should be rebuilt first by clergy familiar with the tradition.
positions.reasons: Rifai-Khuli says their knowledge and concern equip them for the task and compares Tahtawi's clerical mediation of Western ideas.

turns_on: Whether interpretation receives a fixed meaning or is shaped by the interpreter's horizon.

question: What intellectual history does the al-Khuli note give for modern hermeneutics?

positions.position: German modern hermeneutics runs from Schleiermacher through Dilthey and Heidegger to Gadamer; al-Khuli may have encountered it during his stay in Germany.
positions.reasons: Rifai-Khuli recounts al-Khuli's imam posts in Rome and Berlin, his return in 1927, German philosophy's influence, and Shabestari's later Hamburg path. He notes al-Khuli did not document his encounter; Ahmad Khalil identified Schleiermacher parallels, strengthening the author's inference. Heidegger and Gadamer treat understanding as ontological.

turns_on: What influence on al-Khuli can be documented versus inferred.

question: How does مَّا refer to multiple worshipped objects?

positions.position: The relative mā has a collective, plural sense.
positions.reasons: Majaz explicitly analyzes mā as collective.

question: Do Jesus's extraordinary acts amount to independent divine creation?

positions.position: No; Jesus revived the dead and made a bird only through God's power and permission.
positions.reasons: Bursevi says those miracles do not remove Jesus's own incapacity.

question: What ancient witness is sought for the idols' right to worship?

positions.position: A transmitted report from earlier prophets commanding worship of other than God, or ancient learning supporting their right to worship.
positions.reasons: Wahidi-Wajiz specifies a prophetic command; Baydawi accepts ancient learning for either entitlement or command.

positions.position: Inherited knowledge.
positions.reasons: Mawardi transmits Ikrima's gloss without specifying its content.

turns_on: Whether the witness is specified as prophetic instruction or inherited learning in general.

question: What line-drawing identification was transmitted for أَثَٰرَةٍ?

positions.position: Ibn Abbas identified it with lines drawn in earth for Arab divination, and Tabari knew a prophetic interpretation as line-drawing.
positions.reasons: Ibn Atiyya says Arabs used the marks for omens; Tabari promises to cite the report later.
